title: Doubts vanish
hookLine: after awakening he reviews dependent origination, and doubts vanish like mist
tomorrow: In the seen, only the seen

lines: UNDER THE TREE, BY THE RIVER.
THEN, THREE WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.
cards: The book doesn't start with a crowd or a sermon. It starts under a tree. The Buddha has just awakened, at Uruvela, on the bank of the Neranjara river, at the foot of the bodhi tree.
For seven days, the text says, he sits there in one cross-legged posture, feeling the happiness of release. No teaching yet. No students.
Just a man sitting by a river for a week. At the end of those seven days, he does something very specific with his mind, through the watches of the night.

teach.b: In the first watch of the night, he attends to dependent origination in forward order: when this is, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
Ignorance gives rise to formations, formations to consciousness, and so on, link by link, to the whole mass of suffering.
And the verse comes: when things become clear to the one who meditates with ardor, his doubts all vanish, because he understands a thing together with its cause. The next udana: the same, in reverse.
When this is not, that does not come to be; with the ending of this, that ends. Doubts vanish, because he understands the ending of causes. The third: both directions together.
And this time the verse adds an image: he stands, scattering Mara's army, like the sun lighting up the sky. Notice how doubt goes in this story. Not by being argued with, or pushed down.
It goes because something is seen: this comes from that. Elsewhere the early texts list doubt among the hindrances: the wobbling that can't decide. What ends it isn't certainty about everything.
Mist doesn't need to be fought. The sun comes up, and it's gone.

how: Dependent origination is taught across Buddhist schools, and some Theravada chanting books set out its links in forward and reverse order, as in the opening of the Udana.

o: doubt ends when a thing is seen with its cause
doubt ends when you stop asking questions
doubt fades if you ignore it long enough

p: a hindrance: wobbling that can't decide

s: right after awakening, the Buddha began teaching at once
the Udana says he sat for seven days in one posture, feeling the happiness of release.
in the verse, doubts vanish because a thing is understood with its cause
the first udana ties the end of doubt to seeing causes.
the third udana compares him to the sun lighting up the sky
he stands scattering Mara's army, like the sun in the sky.

games.q: you've just awakened, sitting by a river. a week has passed in stillness. what does the Buddha do, in the Udana's first story?
o: walk straight to the nearest town to teach.
attend to how each thing arises from its cause, through the night.
games.why: he reviews dependent origination, forward, then back, then both. after the first two, the verse says his doubts vanish; after the third, he stands like the sun lighting up the sky.

practice: Pick one feeling that's here right now, a bit of tiredness, worry, a flicker of irritation, and ask gently where it came from: a short night, a message you read?
Follow it one link back, then one more if it's there, without analyzing too hard. Just see that this came from that, and notice whether the feeling changes when its cause is seen.

wordCard.voice: Doubts vanish. The first three udanas: when the Buddha sees how each thing arises from its cause, his doubts vanish, and in the third verse he shines like the sun lighting up the sky.

orig.note: Pali kankha: doubt, the wavering that can't decide. in Udana 1.1 the doubts (kankha) all vanish.

carryVoice: Your line: see one cause clearly. Fog thins when the light comes. Day six hundred twelve.
